questions.stem: A 48-year-old man had a kidney transplant 1 year ago after 12 years of hemodialysis. While on dialysis, his calcium was low-normal, his phosphate was high, and his PTH was high. His graft now works well, with a creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL. He reports fatigue and constipation. Today his serum calcium is 11.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is 2.2 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), PTH is 540 pg/mL (normal 10-65), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal. A chest x-ray is normal. Which mechanism best explains his current calcium level?
choices: Tumor secretion of PTH-related peptide
Appropriate PTH response to a low serum calcium
Calcitriol production by activated granuloma macrophages
Autonomous PTH release from long-stimulated glands
Loss-of-function mutation in the calcium-sensing receptor
questions.explanation: Years of CKD (low calcium, high phosphate, low calcitriol) made his parathyroid glands **hyperplastic**, and they now secrete PTH **autonomously**: **tertiary hyperparathyroidism**. The new kidney responds to the high PTH, so calcium rises and phosphate falls. The most tempting choice, an appropriate response to low calcium, describes **secondary** hyperparathyroidism; here calcium is **high**, so PTH is no longer controlled by calcium. With PTHrP or granulomas, PTH would be suppressed.
questions.explanation_pt: Anos de DRC (cálcio baixo, fosfato alto, calcitriol baixo) tornaram as paratireoides **hiperplásicas**, e agora elas secretam PTH de forma **autônoma**: **hiperparatireoidismo terciário**. O enxerto renal responde ao PTH alto, então o cálcio sobe e o fosfato cai. A alternativa mais tentadora, uma resposta adequada ao cálcio baixo, descreve o hiperparatireoidismo **secundário**; aqui o cálcio está **alto**, então o PTH não é mais controlado pelo cálcio. Com PTHrP ou granulomas, o PTH estaria suprimido.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with long-standing heavy alcohol use is admitted after a week of diarrhea and poor food intake. He has a hand tremor, and tapping over his facial nerve makes the corner of his mouth twitch. Serum calcium is 7.0 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5) with albumin of 4.0 g/dL, magnesium is 0.8 mg/dL (normal 1.7-2.2), phosphate is 3.1 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), potassium is 3.2 mEq/L, and lipase is normal. PTH is 14 pg/mL (normal 10-65). He receives intravenous calcium, but his calcium falls again within hours. Which mechanism best explains his persistent hypocalcemia?
choices: Calcium binding to fatty acids in pancreatic fat necrosis
Low magnesium blocking PTH release and PTH action
Autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands
End-organ resistance to PTH from a GNAS mutation
Secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency
questions.explanation: Severe **hypomagnesemia** blocks PTH release from the parathyroid glands and also makes bone and kidney respond poorly to PTH. So PTH stays **inappropriately low-normal**, and calcium (and often potassium) will not stay corrected until **magnesium** is replaced. Vitamin D deficiency is the most tempting choice in a patient with alcohol use, but it would give a **high** PTH, not a low-normal one. Pancreatitis is unlikely with a normal lipase, and a GNAS defect would cause a high PTH. Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism would usually give a **high** phosphate and would not explain why calcium fails to stay corrected with such a low magnesium.
questions.explanation_pt: A **hipomagnesemia** grave bloqueia a liberação de PTH pelas paratireoides e também faz o osso e o rim responderem mal ao PTH. Assim, o PTH fica **inadequadamente normal-baixo**, e o cálcio (e muitas vezes o potássio) não se mantém corrigido até que o **magnésio** seja reposto. A deficiência de vitamina D é a alternativa mais tentadora em um paciente etilista, mas daria PTH **alto**, não normal-baixo. Pancreatite é improvável com lipase normal, e um defeito em GNAS causaria PTH alto. O hipoparatireoidismo autoimune geralmente daria fosfato **alto** e não explicaria por que o cálcio não se mantém corrigido com o magnésio tão baixo.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department during a panic attack. She is breathing fast and deep. She reports numbness around her mouth and in her fingers, and her wrists and fingers are flexed in spasm. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.55 and PaCO2 25 mm Hg. Total serum calcium is 9.3 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), albumin is 4.2 g/dL, and magnesium is normal. Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?
choices: Calcium moving into bone under the action of calcitonin
Suppression of PTH release by the high blood pH
More calcium binding to albumin as H+ leaves it
Calcium loss in the urine caused by bicarbonate excretion
Calcium precipitating with phosphate in soft tissues
questions.explanation: Acute **respiratory alkalosis** lowers the H+ concentration, so hydrogen ions leave the negative sites on **albumin** and calcium binds there instead. **Ionized calcium** falls and causes perioral numbness and **carpopedal spasm**, while the **total calcium** stays normal because only the bound fraction changes. Low PTH is the most tempting choice, but the fall in ionized calcium would increase PTH release, not suppress it. Calcitonin and urinary losses cannot change calcium this fast.
questions.explanation_pt: A **alcalose respiratória** aguda reduz a concentração de H+, então os íons hidrogênio deixam os sítios negativos da **albumina** e o cálcio se liga em seu lugar. O **cálcio ionizado** cai e causa parestesia perioral e **espasmo carpopedal**, enquanto o **cálcio total** permanece normal, pois só a fração ligada muda. O PTH baixo é a alternativa mais tentadora, mas a queda do cálcio ionizado aumentaria a liberação de PTH, e não a suprimiria. A calcitonina e as perdas urinárias não alteram o cálcio tão rápido.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has 3 weeks of nausea, thirst, frequent urination and constipation. He takes several supplements that he buys online. He has no cough, and a chest x-ray shows normal lungs and no hilar lymph nodes. Laboratory results: serum calcium 12.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate 5.0 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), PTH 5 pg/mL (normal 10-65), PTH-related peptide undetectable, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 240 ng/mL (normal 30-100), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D at the upper limit of normal. Creatinine is mildly elevated. What is the most likely cause of his hypercalcemia?
choices: Excess intake of vitamin D
Granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis
Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
Primary hyperparathyroidism
questions.explanation: A very high **25-hydroxyvitamin D** with suppressed PTH and **high phosphate** points to **vitamin D intoxication** from supplements. Vitamin D raises gut absorption of both calcium and phosphate, and the high calcium suppresses PTH. At very high levels, 25-OH vitamin D itself activates the vitamin D receptor, so 1,25 does not need to be high. Sarcoidosis is the most tempting choice, but granulomas make excess **1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D**, so 25-OH vitamin D is normal and 1,25 is high; his lungs and hilum are also normal. Primary hyperparathyroidism and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) would not give a suppressed PTH.
questions.explanation_pt: A **25-hidroxivitamina D** muito alta com PTH suprimido e **fosfato alto** indica **intoxicação por vitamina D** por suplementos. A vitamina D aumenta a absorção intestinal de cálcio e de fosfato, e o cálcio alto suprime o PTH. Em níveis muito altos, a própria 25-OH vitamina D ativa o receptor de vitamina D, então a 1,25 não precisa estar alta. A sarcoidose é a alternativa mais tentadora, mas os granulomas produzem excesso de **1,25-di-hidroxivitamina D**, então a 25-OH vitamina D fica normal e a 1,25 fica alta; além disso, os pulmões e os hilos dele são normais. O hiperparatireoidismo primário e a hipercalcemia hipocalciúrica familiar (HHF) não dariam PTH suprimido.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for short stature. He has a round face, a stocky build, and short fourth and fifth metacarpals. Serum calcium, phosphate and PTH are all normal. Genetic testing shows an inactivating mutation in GNAS that he inherited from his father, who has the same body features and normal laboratory results. A cousin with the same body features has hypocalcemia and a high PTH; her mutation came from her mother. Which mechanism best explains why this boy's kidneys respond normally to PTH?
choices: Proximal tubule cells express mainly the maternal GNAS allele
The paternal GNAS allele is silenced in every tissue of the body
Somatic mosaicism limits his mutation to bone and connective tissue
His mutation affects the PTH receptor but leaves Gs-alpha working
Extra calcitriol from his kidneys overcomes a partial PTH resistance
questions.explanation: This is **pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism**. **GNAS** is **imprinted**: in the **renal proximal tubule**, Gs-alpha comes mainly from the **maternal** allele, so a mutation from the father leaves the PTH response intact and labs stay normal. In most other tissues both alleles work, so losing one copy still causes the **Albright hereditary osteodystrophy** features. The most tempting choice, silencing of the paternal allele in every tissue, cannot be right, because then his paternal mutation would cause no body features at all; his cousin's maternal mutation causes **pseudohypoparathyroidism 1A**.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **pseudopseudo-hipoparatireoidismo**. O **GNAS** sofre **imprinting**: no **túbulo proximal renal**, a Gs-alfa vem principalmente do alelo **materno**, então uma mutação herdada do pai preserva a resposta ao PTH e os exames ficam normais. Na maioria dos outros tecidos os dois alelos funcionam, então a perda de uma cópia ainda causa as características físicas da **osteodistrofia hereditária de Albright**. A alternativa mais tentadora, silenciamento do alelo paterno em todos os tecidos, não pode estar certa, pois então a mutação paterna não causaria nenhuma alteração física; a mutação materna da prima causa **pseudo-hipoparatireoidismo 1A**.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl is brought in after a seizure. Since age 4 she has had repeated oral thrush and fungal infections of her nails that return after treatment. Her older brother has adrenal insufficiency. She has no heart disease, and her early childhood growth was normal. Serum calcium is 6.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is 7.0 mg/dL (normal for age 3.7-5.6), magnesium is normal, and PTH is undetectable. Her parents are healthy. A mutation in which gene most likely explains her condition?
choices: TBX1
GNAS
FOXP3
AIRE
CASR
questions.explanation: Chronic **mucocutaneous candidiasis**, **hypoparathyroidism** and adrenal insufficiency (**Addison disease**) in siblings with healthy parents fit **autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1**, an autosomal recessive defect in **AIRE**. Without AIRE, thymic medullary cells do not display tissue antigens, so self-reactive T cells escape negative selection. DiGeorge syndrome (**TBX1**, 22q11.2) is the most tempting choice because it also causes low PTH and infections, but it usually presents in the newborn period with heart defects. FOXP3 (IPEX, X-linked, so seen in boys) and activating CASR mutations do not explain chronic candidiasis with adrenal failure.
questions.explanation_pt: **Candidíase mucocutânea crônica**, **hipoparatireoidismo** e insuficiência adrenal (**doença de Addison**) em irmãos com pais saudáveis indicam **síndrome poliglandular autoimune tipo 1**, um defeito autossômico recessivo do **AIRE**. Sem o AIRE, as células da medula tímica não exibem antígenos de tecidos, e linfócitos T autorreativos escapam da seleção negativa. A síndrome de DiGeorge (**TBX1**, 22q11.2) é a alternativa mais tentadora, pois também causa PTH baixo e infecções, mas costuma se manifestar no período neonatal, com defeitos cardíacos. Mutações em FOXP3 (IPEX, ligada ao X, portanto em meninos) e mutações ativadoras do CASR não explicam candidíase crônica com insuficiência adrenal.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman had years of untreated primary hyperparathyroidism with bone pain. Before surgery her alkaline phosphatase was very high, and x-rays showed subperiosteal bone loss in the fingers and lytic jaw lesions. A large parathyroid adenoma is removed. On the third day after surgery she has tingling in her fingers and around her mouth. Serum calcium is 7.1 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is 1.9 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), magnesium is 1.3 mg/dL (normal 1.7-2.2), and PTH is 28 pg/mL (normal 10-65). Albumin is normal. Which mechanism best explains her low calcium?
choices: Permanent damage to the remaining parathyroid glands
Fast mineral uptake by bone that was heavily resorbed
Release of stored calcitonin from the manipulated thyroid
New PTH resistance in the kidney and bone
Calcium binding to citrate in transfused blood products
questions.explanation: After a long-standing PTH excess is removed, the heavily resorbed bone (**osteitis fibrosa cystica**) quickly takes up **calcium, phosphate and magnesium**: **hungry bone syndrome**. This explains why all three minerals are low while PTH is in the normal range. Permanent hypoparathyroidism is the most tempting choice, but it causes a **high** phosphate and a low PTH. PTH resistance would give a high PTH, and calcitonin has little effect on calcium in humans.
questions.explanation_pt: Após a retirada de um excesso prolongado de PTH, o osso muito reabsorvido (**osteíte fibrosa cística**) capta rapidamente **cálcio, fosfato e magnésio**: **síndrome da fome óssea** (*hungry bone*). Isso explica por que os três minerais estão baixos enquanto o PTH está na faixa normal. O hipoparatireoidismo permanente é a alternativa mais tentadora, mas causa fosfato **alto** e PTH baixo. A resistência ao PTH daria PTH alto, e a calcitonina tem pouco efeito sobre o cálcio em humanos.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman treated for breast cancer 4 years ago has 2 months of back and rib pain. In the last week she has become confused and very thirsty. Serum calcium is 13.2 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5), phosphate is 4.1 mg/dL (normal 2.5-4.5), PTH is 7 pg/mL (normal 10-65), PTH-related peptide is undetectable, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low-normal. Imaging shows multiple lytic lesions in the spine, ribs and pelvis. Which mechanism best explains her hypercalcemia?
choices: Tumor secretion of PTH-related peptide into the blood
Calcitriol production by tumor cells
Local osteoclast activation by tumor cells in bone
Autonomous PTH secretion by a parathyroid adenoma
Increased renal calcium reabsorption from a thiazide
questions.explanation: Tumor cells that grow in bone release local factors that raise **RANKL** and activate **osteoclasts**, so bone is destroyed and calcium is released: **osteolytic metastases**. The high calcium suppresses PTH and calcitriol. Humoral hypercalcemia from **PTHrP** is the most tempting choice in a cancer patient, but the blood PTHrP is undetectable, and PTHrP would usually lower phosphate. Calcitriol-producing tumors (some lymphomas) would show a high 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
questions.explanation_pt: Células tumorais que crescem no osso liberam fatores locais que aumentam o **RANKL** e ativam os **osteoclastos**, então o osso é destruído e o cálcio é liberado: **metástases osteolíticas**. O cálcio alto suprime o PTH e o calcitriol. A hipercalcemia humoral por **PTHrP** é a alternativa mais tentadora em paciente oncológica, mas o PTHrP sérico é indetectável, e o PTHrP geralmente reduziria o fosfato. Tumores que produzem calcitriol (alguns linfomas) mostrariam 1,25-di-hidroxivitamina D alta.
